paragraphs.text: In May 1845, two wooden ships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, left London bound for the Arctic. John Franklin, the leader of the expedition, captained one ship while Francis Crozier commanded the other. Their mission was to find the fabled Northwest Passage — the shortcut between Britain and Asia around northern Canada. And with only 500 kilometres of mainland Arctic coastline left for them to explore, success seemed guaranteed.

But they never returned, and the British government announced a £20,000 reward — half for finding the ships and half for navigating the Northwest Passage. Dozens of ‘rescue’ expeditions took up the challenge, but it wasn’t until almost 15 years later that the grim fate of Franklin, Crozier and 129 crew was finally revealed.

A note found on King William Island in the Canadian Arctic detailed how their ships had become trapped in ice, how 24 men, including Franklin, had died, and how the others had attempted to march across the frozen landscape to reach help. None of them survived. But questions still remained: why had some of Britain’s most competent sailors and explorers been unable to survive in the region, and what had happened to the two ships?

A team of Canadian scientists, led by marine archaeologist Robert Grenier, is now attempting to answer these questions. And, with the help of local Inuit man Louie Kamookak, who has been recording Inuit testimonies about encounters with explorers for more than 30 years, they have traced the final movements of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror. And the Inuit testimonies, which include walking out across the frozen sea to a ship and exploring its interior, have recently been backed up by artefacts that Grenier and his team have found on nearby beaches.

‘We found a series of copper fragments,’ Grenier says. He believes they probably came from one of the ships. More importantly, the fragments aren’t corroded in the way that they probably would be if they had spent more than 100 years under water, and some have been fashioned into Inuit tools. Consequently, Grenier believes these fragments were probably salvaged by the Inuit from one of Franklin’s ships just before it sank. And that might mean there’s a ship nearby.

The next stage is to find the actual wreck. Usually, a magnetometer is used to pinpoint sunken ships via the large amounts of metal they contain, but in this case the readings have proved useless. ‘The Arctic geology is very peculiar. The magnetic signals you get from the land up there are so strong,’ Grenier explains. Instead, they’re relying on sonar. He hopes that finding one or both of the ships will help to explain why the extremely capable men of the Franklin expedition failed to survive. So far, the most plausible explanation has been put forward by Owen Beattie, a Canadian anthropologist. He carried out tests on the bodies of three men who were buried in the ice after dying early on during the Franklin expedition, and found that they contained astonishingly high levels of lead.

The discovery was a breakthrough: if Franklin’s men were suffering from lead poisoning, which can cause, among other things, fatigue and memory loss, they would have found it difficult to carry out the everyday tasks needed to survive in the Arctic, and been susceptible to disease. At the time, Beattie thought the lead poisoning was caused by tins of food that had been manufactured badly and had contaminated the food, but Franklin researcher William Battersby believes that there might be another explanation.

According to Battersby’s research, a firm called Goldner supplied more than 15 tonnes of tinned meat to the Franklin expedition. Between 1845 and 1851, the same firm supplied the Royal Navy with more than 1,200 tonnes of tinned meat. If Goldner had been producing tainted meat in 1845, Battersby argues, it’s difficult to see how it could have spent the next seven years getting repeat orders from the Navy.

Eventually, after examining the lives of the sailors to see if they had any common heritage that could account for high levels of lead in their bodies — they didn’t — Battersby realised that the only thing that was different about the Franklin expedition was the presence of engines to power the ships.

It turns out that the system used to feed the engines with water also provided drinking water for the men, through what was probably a maze of lead piping. Battersby believes that this piping was responsible for the lead poisoning. He says his theory is supported by the unusual nature of the food supplies of the ships, which consisted of a high level of concentrated ingredients — from soups and flour to rum — that would have been made up using the plentiful water on board.

For Kamookak, a wreck discovery would prove the accuracy of Inuit history. Many of the oral testimonies he has gathered from the Inuit elders have matched up almost exactly with the accepted written history. Collecting the material proved surprisingly easy — once word got around that there was someone who would listen to them, the Inuit themselves tracked him down.
Kamookak explains that for the Inuit, stories have always been a way of passing on survival skills and entertaining each other through the months of darkness.

Grenier hopes that the discovery of one or both of the wrecks will have advantages for the region. He’s keen to find the ships before anyone else does, because he wants to make sure they're properly protected, and hopes that they will become an attraction that can benefit the Inuit.
